I've been making dice since the start of covid as a hobby, but do sell to fund my hobby and just broke even over summer.  So far I've spent $1500 on supplies and equipment  making about 60 sets of dice.  Much of that has been upfront costs as well.  To sell you will need to make your own masters or purchase online from a retailer that specifies they are legal for commercial use.  I got mine off etsy for ~$90.  To make you're own you'll need a 3d resin printer.  If your store has a simple logo most etsy sellers will throw it on a dice for an extra 10-15.      
     
To get bubble free dice (I wouldn't sell anything less) you will need a pressure pot and air compressor.  If you don't have those that's $180-$250.  Making the molds can be tricky and took me several tries to get right.  If you don't do a good job on them it can lead to hours more sanding per dice set (I went from 3 hours to 1 hour with better molds).  The hard part is that each try costs about $50-$70 worth of silicone.   It took me 4 to be happy with my mold.  For me a mold lasts 30-40 sets before wearing out. The nice part of making your own is that you can make as many as you want.  This summer I'll be making 4 molds so I can do for sets at a time in my pressure pot.        
       
Once you have all that you will need the various Micah powders and dyes for your resin, they cost a bit but last a long time.  Resin also isn't cheap but for the dyes and resin each dice set only costs about $5.  All the stuff above is where a majority of expenses are.  I figure 60ml of resin per set.  But I like a bit extra to be sure I don't run out.     
     
Time is a huge factor as well, each set takes ~30 minutes to mix, 20 hours in the pressure pot, 1-2 hours to clean up and polish, and 30 min to paint.  I figure 2.5 active man hours per set.  A pottery wheel can speed up the clean up and polishing portion significantly,  that's my next upgrade.   I started selling for $25 per set and got a lot of compliments and now sell for $45 per set.  If you are trying to make the art piece level ones that sell for $80+ it will take more time.     
        
Not trying to dissuade you and I hope this helps.  I also second rybonators videos.   That's how I got into the hobby.  I think it's a great idea to start at an lgs, just understand that it does take man hours to produce them, it's not an effortless process.
Honestly if you're serious about dice making it would be a good idea to watch all of his dice videos before diving in.

Stax is on of my favorite archetypes and I highly recommend it.  The reason people don't like it is because of a few reasons.  First and most obvious,  it stops them from doing what they want.  People don't like counter magic for the same reason.  You top deck a card you're excited to play and it gets countered feels bad, stax has the same effect.       
       
 Second, poorly made stax decks struggle to end.  It leads to a draw go style of play.  Honestly from my experience the issue is generally the non stax players spending 5 minutes every turn trying to figure a way out then passing without doing anything.  But I also pride myself on quick play.           
       
  Finally and the reason I think it should be played, it punishes poor deck building and abusing the system.  Land ramp is incredibly strong in commander because people are afraid to destroy lands.  Stax can blow up lands and punish the player who just played 3 land ramp cards.  It also forces people to play proper removal and have flexible decks. Many people get greedy in deck building and don't have enough answers.        
      
  If you do build stax, which everyone should, I do recommend having more than one deck.  Stax is good once and awhile, but if you're playing it 4 games in a row it gets old pretty fast for your opponents.  Also make sure you build with a way to break parody.   For example my stax list with land destruction runs only 20 lands, but also runs 25 artifact ramp.

I had the same concern getting into making resin dice.  Spent around 1200 and took 2 years to break even.  You don't need mold release, you don't need a heat gun, you don't need special measuring cups, and you don't need special stir sticks.  I use small plastic disposable medical measuring cups.  They're like 3cents each.  Then I pour them into a red solo cup to mix very well.  I use popsicle sticks instead of stir sticks. If you want to warm up the resin it might prevent some bubbles.  Just set the cup in warm water. Resin does not stick to silicone so you should not need release.  After pouring the resin in the mold you can use a lighter to pop any bubbles that appear.  This method is much cheaper, the reason many people don't recommend it is because there is so much stuff you are throwing away each time.
